title: Errors and Exceptions
summary: An exception is a signal that something went wrong while a program was running.
introduction: An exception is a signal that something went wrong while a program was running. Read the message to find the problem. Then use try and except when your program can give a helpful response to that problem.
learningObjectives: Read a traceback from the bottom up and locate the failing line
Catch specific exceptions with try and except and use the exception object
Run clean-up code with finally and success-only code with else
Raise built-in exceptions and define custom exception classes

blocks.text: Two kinds of problem stop a program. A **syntax error** means Python could not even parse the file, so nothing runs; fix the line it points at. An **exception** happens while the program runs, when an operation cannot complete. Both produce a traceback, and reading one is the first debugging skill.

blocks.title: divide.py
blocks.code:
def divide(a, b):
    return a / b

print(divide(10, 2))
print(divide(10, 0))
print("done")

blocks.title: python divide.py
blocks.content:
5.0
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/ada/projects/divide.py", line 5, in <module>
    print(divide(10, 0))
          ~~~~~~^^^^^^^
  File "/home/ada/projects/divide.py", line 2, in divide
    return a / b
           ~~^~~
ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

blocks.text: Read it from the bottom: the last line gives the exception type and message. Above it, the frames show the path the program took to get there, most recent call last: line 5 called `divide`, and line 2 inside `divide` failed, with markers under the exact expression. Note that `done` was never printed; an unhandled exception ends the program.

blocks.title: safe_divide.py
python safe_divide.py
blocks.content:
5.0
Cannot divide by zero
None
Parsed 12
Skipping 'x': invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'x'
Skipping '7.5': invalid literal for int() with base 10: '7.5'

blocks.text: Python runs the `try` block; if the named exception occurs anywhere inside it, execution jumps to the matching `except` block and then continues after the whole statement. `as error` binds the exception object so you can print its message. The optional `else` block runs only when no exception occurred, which keeps the `try` block small and the success path obvious.

blocks.title: several.py
python several.py
blocks.content:
Bad value: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'two'
0
Missing field: 'quantity'
0
15.0

blocks.text: `except` clauses are tested in order, and a tuple catches several types with one handler. Exceptions form a hierarchy: `ValueError` and `KeyError` both derive from `Exception`, so `except Exception` would catch either. Catch the most specific type you actually know how to handle.

blocks.title: A bare except hides bugs
blocks.text: `except:` with no type catches *everything*, including the `KeyboardInterrupt` that Ctrl+C sends, and `except Exception:` wrapped around a large block is nearly as bad: both also swallow typos in variable names (`NameError`) and every other bug inside the block. The program then limps on with wrong data and the real bug surfaces somewhere else. Name the exceptions you expect, keep `try` blocks short, and if you must catch everything, log the traceback and re-raise with a bare `raise`.

Closing settings.json

blocks.text: `finally` runs no matter how the `try` block ends: normally, through `return`, or by an exception that is propagating upwards. It is the place for clean-up such as closing files and network connections; notice that `Closing` is printed before the returned dictionary. For files specifically, the `with` statement in [Reading and Writing Files](/tutorials/python/file-handling) does that clean-up automatically.

blocks.title: raising.py
python raising.py
blocks.content:
70
Invalid: amount must be positive
Declined: balance 100 is less than 500

blocks.text: `raise` signals that *your* function cannot continue; the caller decides what to do about it. Use the built-in types when they fit: `ValueError` for bad values, `TypeError` for wrong types, `KeyError` or `LookupError` for missing things. Define a custom class derived from `Exception` when callers need to tell your error apart from everything else; a class body holding only a docstring is enough, and [Classes and Objects](/tutorials/python/classes-objects) explains the syntax.

rows: A variable or function name is not defined (often a typo)
An operation gets the wrong type, such as `"3" + 4`
The type is right but the value is not, such as `int("abc")`
A missing dictionary key or a list index out of range
An object has no such attribute or method
A path does not exist when opening a file

blocks.title: Did you mean?
blocks.text: Since Python 3.10 many tracebacks end with a suggestion, such as `NameError: name 'nme' is not defined. Did you mean: 'name'?`, and Python 3.13 colours tracebacks in the terminal. Read the whole last line before searching the web; the answer is often right there.

questions.question: What does this program print?
questions.explanation: `int("42")` succeeds, so the `try` block prints 42, the `else` block runs because nothing was raised, and `finally` always runs last.

questions.question: Which `except` clause handles the error raised by `int("abc")`?
questions.explanation: The argument has the right type (a string) but an unusable value, so Python raises `ValueError`.

seo.title: Python Exceptions – try, except, else, finally and raise
seo.description: Learn to read Python tracebacks, catch exceptions with try and except, use else and finally, raise built-in errors and define custom exception classes.
